title: Flex container and items
learningObjectives: Explain flex container and items and build a practical layout with it.

understand.concept: Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout system. Setting display:flex or inline-flex on a container makes its in-flow children flex items. The container controls the flex formatting context and the items participate in flexible sizing and alignment.
understand.whyItMatters: Flexbox is useful for arranging items in a row or column and distributing available space. It reduces reliance on manual margins and positioning for common component layouts.
understand.analogy: A flex container is like a row of movable cards that can share space and align along a chosen direction.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is simplified; actual flex layout follows the flex formatting algorithm and writing-mode rules.

explain.narrative: The three buttons become flex items and sit in a row with a consistent gap.

examples.explanation: The three buttons become flex items and sit in a row with a consistent gap.
examples.expectedOutput: A browser-rendered demonstration of the layout concept.

practise.guidedTask: Create a toolbar with four items. Switch the container between display:flex and display:block and compare.
practise.independentTask: Build a responsive component using this concept. Test long labels, narrow widths, and keyboard navigation.
hints: Inspect the flex container and items in developer tools.
Change one axis or alignment property at a time.
Test with translated or longer labels.

questions.prompt: Which declaration creates a flex formatting context for a container?
questions.explanation: display:flex establishes a flex container for its in-flow children.

questions.prompt: What should you check when changing flex-direction?
options: How the main and cross axes change
questions.answer: How the main and cross axes change
questions.explanation: Flex alignment is defined relative to the main and cross axes.
